Screened Electrification Equipment - v2#

Date: 2026-10-12

In brief. Electricity demand is growing faster than the grid can carry it. Regulated utilities pay for the new wires, transformers and substations. Equipment makers and contractors that supply them are paid as the work is delivered. The strategy takes advantage of the opposite positioning on the balance sheet. It holds the best-scoring the suppliers and shorts the weakest of electrification companies, mostly the utilities and pipelines doing the paying. The selection is based on a consolidated score of fourteen measures (power market sensitivity, capital intensity, revenue growth/acceleration, earnings and revenue surprises, and price trends).

The grid stress that took hold in 2023 looks durable.* Utilities have committed to multi-year capital plans, equipment lead times run to years, and real yields remain elevated. The suppliers' own filings show no slowdown: their median revenue growth is 12.0% a year after inflation and still accelerating, the fastest since early 2023. Over that period the long/short has delivered a Sharpe ratio of 2.28 after trading costs, with a beta of 0.47 to the S&P 500.

This is a regime-dependent strategy that will profit during the grid-stress regime. The strategy writeup includes some gradual/partial mitigants and a full step-aside.

*An inidicative public signal came on 29 November 2022, when PJM, the grid operator for 13 mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states and DC, added a separate "Data Centers" adjustment to its load forecast for the AEP, APS and Dominion utility zones. Its January 2023 forecast raised the data-center load it expects by 2030 from 4.8 GW to 12.8 GW; the January 2025 forecast raised it to 32.8 GW.

Sharpe uses a flat 4.0% risk-free rate. Returns are total returns, dividends reinvested. The strategy's figures are after 10bp on every trade — long and short name changes, resizing, sleeve and short resets, and each step-aside switch — and 1% a year borrow on the short (Costs); the "before trading costs" row removes the 10bp. ETF returns are net of their own fees. Max time under water is the longest stretch below a previous peak within the window; "+" means the drawdown was still unrecovered at the end of 2022.

This is a grid-tightness strategy. It does not work well when the grid has ample spare capacity. The strategy deals with this in 4 ways:

Partial/Gradual

  1. Stretch de-lever: When the book runs more than 15% above its 200-day average, it is cut to 80% and the rest earns T-bill interest. This is intended to slow down when the book is more likely to be near the peak.
  2. Volatility target: When markets become choppy, it targets a 20% vol target for the book and moves the rest into T-bills. This is intended to guard against a sharp change into an oversupplied grid regime.
  3. The strategy inherently rotates toward suppliers whose sales are still growing.

Full switch-off

  1. Step-aside: the whole portfolio goes into T-bills whenever the either the real yield is below zero or suppliers' real revenue growth is below zero (in plot, regime strip isn't green).

Since 2023 the strategy leads every benchmark on every measure but one — time unnder water. (But before 2023, this was not the appropriate grid-tightness regime that would serve the strategy well)

Portfolio Construction#

Both long and short legs begin by restricting to reasonably liquid eqectrical equipment and power related names (by industry code and keyword). The long leg restricts further to supplier (not owner), profitable, non-subsidy. the short book chooses its candidates from teh rest. For both we develop a score as in the table below. The long book holds the top portion (half) of its screened suppliers, the short the bottom portion (fifth) of its eligible set. The long book adds risk control, and one rule decides when to step aside.

Aspect Long book Short book Source
SCREEN
 Electrification population Companies in the SEC's electrical-equipment and power industry codes, plus nuclear fuel-cycle names found by keyword; at least $10m of stock traded on a typical day over the past year and a full year of price history (about 200 names)
  • Industry codes: SEC EDGAR
  • Keywords: SEC EDGAR full-text search
  • Prices and volume: Yahoo Finance
On-theme The 10-K annual report used data center, substation, switchgear, transmission and distribution, grid modernization or electric utilities in the previous four years. Data center counts only where the business description uses it for customers or markets, not for the company's own IT systems. Gas pipeline and gas distribution companies don't qualify: their transmission and distribution is gas, not the power grid SEC EDGAR full-text search of 10-Ks
Supplier, not owner Capital spending ÷ sales in the lightest 60% of the population, which separates suppliers from the utilities that own the wires -- SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
Profitable Trailing-12-month net income above zero, using only figures already filed at the time -- SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
Not subsidy-dependent No 10-K in the previous four years mentions the investment tax credit, production tax credit, advanced manufacturing production credit or net energy metering -- SEC EDGAR full-text search of 10-Ks
Not held long -- A company cannot be long and short at once: names the long book holds are removed before the short basket is picked --
RANK
 One score
  • From filings: capital intensity, revenue acceleration, revenue growth, revenue and earnings surprises, growth in capital spending
  • From prices: 12-month momentum, 1-month reversal
  • From power markets: two signals for each measure below: the stock's 36-month sensitivity to its shocks (who benefits structurally) and that sensitivity × the latest 3-month shock (who is benefiting right now)
    • Wholesale prices: mean day-ahead LMP, PJM hubs and ERCOT hub; benefits from higher power prices
    • Congestion: mean absolute day-ahead congestion, PJM zones; benefits from a constrained grid
    • Scarcity: 99th-percentile hourly day-ahead price, ERCOT hub; benefits from price spikes
  • Average the fourteen standardised scores
  • Filings: SEC EDGAR XBRL filings
  • Prices: Yahoo Finance
  • Power: PJM and ERCOT day-ahead market prices
Selection Hold the top half each quarter; a held name stays while in the top 65% Short the bottom fifth, re-formed each quarter (13 names on average, never fewer than 10, 18 today) --
WEIGHT
 Equal weight Each name weighted equally Each name weighted equally; $0.25 short for every $1 of capital, reset each month --
RISK CONTROL
 Volatility target Size the book daily to target 20% annual volatility, never above 1.5×; resize only on moves of more than 20 points of exposure None of its own: the short stays at $0.25 per $1 of capital while these controls shrink the long side, so the book moves toward market-neutral as it de-risks --
Stretch de-lever Cut to 80% when the book is over 15% above its 200-day average or far ahead of the market; 60% at extremes --
Gold / Treasury sleeve 15% in GLD and IEF, reset monthly as a macro hedge against growth scares --

Shaded cells span both books: the rule is the same for each.

Every input is point in time: company figures are used only after they were filed, the 10-K keyword checks read only filings made before each year's screen, CPI is lagged a month for its release date, and the real yield and supplier growth enter the step-aside rule a day late.

Return Attribution#

Compared with Theme (GRID) or Market (SPY)#

To attribute the sources of return, we conduct some simple regression of the strategy's daily return on GRID or SPY. Whatever is left (the regression intercept) after accounting for exposure to the theme (or in case of SPY, the market) is alpha. A t-statistic above 2 means the result is unlikely to be by chance alone.

2023 – Aug 2026 alpha per year t-statistic
Long/short vs GRID 24.5% 4.3
Long/short vs S&P 500 23.5% 3.9
Ranking alone: top half vs all qualifying names, equally weighted 9.3% 3.5
  • Strategy alpha survives the short. About 24.5% a year of return is not explained by moving with GRID (beta 0.40 to GRID). The short removes theme exposure; what remains comes from the sources below.
  • The alpha is statistically strong: a t-statistic of 4.3 against GRID and 3.9 against the S&P 500.
  • To test whether the ranking adds value, we regress the long book's daily return on that of the same book holding every name that passes the screen in equal weight, with identical risk controls. The intercept, 9.3% a year since 2023 (t-stat 3.5), is the value added from picking the top half of the screened names.

Sources of the Alpha#

We can decompose the strategy's daily return splits into the components below.

Each day the strategy's return is

r = (1−w)·[h·R + (1−h)·rf] + w·S − s·B − s·borrow − costs

where R is the long arm's return, h the long exposure set by the risk controls, rf the daily cash rate, w the macro sleeve weight (15%) and S its return, s the short size (0.25) and B the short basket's return. Writing h as the average exposure h̄ (0.611) plus the day's deviation from it, h̄ + (h − h̄), splits the long part in three:

r = (1−w)·[h·R + rf − h·rf] + w·S − s·B − s·borrow − costs

  = (1−w)·[(h̄ + (h − h̄))·R + rf − (h̄ + (h − h̄))·rf] + …

  = (1−w)·[h̄·R + (h − h̄)·R + rf − h̄·rf − (h − h̄)·rf] + …

  = (1−w)·[(h̄·R + rf − h̄·rf) + ((h − h̄)·R − (h − h̄)·rf)] + …

  = (1−w)·[h̄·R + (1 − h̄)·rf + (h − h̄)·(R − rf)] + …

r = (1−w)·h̄·R + (1−w)·(1−h̄)·rf + (1−w)·(h−h̄)·(R−rf) + w·S − s·B − s·borrow − costs

The seven terms, in order, are long selection, cash, timing, sleeve, short, borrow and costs:

piece daily formula
Long stock selection (1−w) · h̄ · R
Cash interest (1−w) · (1−h̄) · rf
Risk-control timing (1−w) · (h − h̄) · (R − rf)
Gold/Treasury sleeve w · S
Short − s · B
Short borrow − s · 1% ÷ 252
Trading costs − 10bp × amount traded

Each piece's daily series is regressed on GRID's daily return; its intercept × 252 is the alpha in the table. The pieces sum to the strategy's return every day, so their alphas sum to the total.

2023 – Aug 2026 alpha per year, ex-GRID share

Short stock selection: the shorted names doing worse than their theme exposure implies 4.0% 16%
Risk-control timing: volatility target and stretch cut, versus holding the average size throughout 6.5% 27%

Cash interest on the part the risk controls keep out of stocks 1.3% 5%

  • Share is the component's alpha divided by total alpha of 24.5%.
  • About two-thirds is stock selection (16 points, long and short together).
  • Per dollar, the long names beat their GRID exposure by 22.4%. Multiply by 0.85 outside macro sleeve and 0.611 (average exposure) and you get to 0.52. Then 0.52 x 22.4 ~ 11.6 (11.7 in the table).
  • The shorted names returned 15.8% a year less than their GRID exposure predicted, good for the strategy as we are short them. The strategy size the short at 0.25 per dollar. This is about 4.0% (the short selection line). The short earns positive alpha (4.0%) even though it lost a little money (about −1% a year): by removing theme exposure it gives up GRID-driven return, and what it contributes beyond that is positive.
  • Part of the alpha is choosing which corner of the theme to own (capital-light, profitable, on-theme suppliers); the ranking within that corner adds about 9 points a year (t ≈ 3.5) over holding every qualifying name equally.
  • About a quarter is timing from the risk controls (6.5 points): the book was larger when markets were calm and smaller when they were volatile or stretched.
  • The gold/Treasury sleeve and cash add about 3 points: their returns are unrelated to GRID.

  • Controlling for academic style factors leaves 20.7% of alpha, and for ETF styles leaves 25.4%. The tilts largely cancel: momentum added about 1.2 points a year while the small-cap and profitability tilts cost about 1.9.
  • The book does lean on some styles:
  • Momentum: clearly positive (a loading of 0.23 on the academic momentum factor or 0.07 on the ETF measure, meaning the book tends to move about a quarter as much as the momentum factor). This is the one that matters: if momentum stocks sell off sharply, the strategy will likely fall with them (see Momentum Sell-Offs below).
  • Small size and profitability/quality: moderate tilts. That fits the rules, which pick profitable, capital-light mid-caps.
  • Growth vs value:* a slight tilt toward growth on both measures (0.15 on ETF, -0.08 on academic value factor). These are small enough so that we are reasonably comfortable that the strategy isn't a disguised growth bet.
  • Low volatility: it leans away from low-volatility stocks.
  • Most of the return is not style: the factors explain less than half of the daily variation (R² 0.44–0.47).

Episodes are peak-to-trough falls of at least 7% in the Fama-French momentum factor, plus July 2024 (when the MTUM ETF fell 13%) and the DeepSeek day (a shock to the AI-power theme). The strategy held T-bills from November 2019 to April 2022 under the step-aside rule.   • Momentum sell-offs come in two kinds. In most of them (2019, 2020–21, mid-2022, early 2023) momentum fell because beaten-down stocks rebounded in a rising market. The strategy stayed positive every time it was invested but lagged GRID, PAVE and the S&P 500, because its low beta and the short side cap its upside. Had the step-aside rule kept it invested through 2020–21, it would still have made money in all three of that period's crashes (2.3% to 6.2%), though far behind GRID and PAVE.
  • In sell-offs in a falling market it generally lost less than GRID: −3.1% against −8.9% in July 2024, −4.8% against −5.5% in February–March 2025 and −1.8% against −9.3% in June–August 2026, but slightly more on the DeepSeek day (−5.9% against −5.6%).
  • Its largest loss in any episode is −5.9%, on the DeepSeek day.

Short Book Detail#

Short Basket Composition#

The shorted stocks rose 4.0% a year over the full period, against 20.8% for PAVE, with a worst fall of −52%. They move with the theme, so the short gains when the theme falls and cushions the long book. They have also risen far less than the theme, so in a rising market the short costs much less than the long book earns.

Rationale for the Short#

As is desirable of short legs, the short doesn't need its member names to fall always but only to do worse than the long book. The proposed strategy accomplishes this. The long book has beaten the shorted stocks in both rising and falling months (by 5.1% a month when GRID fell and 1.1% when it rose).

2023 – Aug 2026, average month shorted stocks long book long book − 0.25 × shorted stocks GRID
GRID down (17 months) −6.0% −0.9% 0.6% −3.8%
GRID up (27 months) 4.2% 5.3% 4.2% 5.5%
All months (44) 0.2% 2.9% 2.8% 1.9%

Long book: the long side with its risk controls, before the short. Best in each row in bold, between the last two columns.

The short costs about 1 point of return a year (39.5% to 38.6% since 2023), and in exchange cuts the worst drawdown from −16.0% to −8.5% and beta to the S&P 500 from 0.72 to 0.47, raising the Sharpe ratio from 1.93 to 2.28. In months when GRID fell, the strategy was slightly positive.

It is weakest when beaten-down stocks rebound sharply. The shorted stocks are largely recent laggards, so when laggards rally, as in mid-2020 and mid-2022, they rose 22–29% in a few weeks and the short cost money. In falling-market sell-offs it helped: in February–March 2025 the shorted stocks fell 12.3% and the short cut the book's loss from −7.6% to −4.8%.

group names why they rank low
Electric utilities (8) BKH · CNP · EIX · ES · OGE · PCG · POR · TXNM Own the wires: capital spending a quarter to half of sales

About 60% of the basket, on average since 2019, is utilities and power producers — the companies paying for the buildout. The rest are electrification industrials that the buildout is passing by. Gas pipelines and gas distributors are not shorted: their "transmission and distribution" is gas, not the power grid.

PAVE Alternative#

PAVE is the simple alternative. A $0.25 short of the PAVE ETF (US infrastructure and electrical companies — closest in make-up to the long book) gives a similar result under the same rules: Sharpe 1.26 over the full period and 2.06 since 2023 (against 1.43 and 2.28), with a worst fall of −11.7% against −12.1%. It is one liquid line ($13.5bn fund, about $82m traded a day, listed options), normally cheap to borrow — no single-name borrow to arrange. We prefer the single-name short because its edge is in stock selection rather than index tracking; an investor who values simplicity gives up some return per unit of risk with PAVE.

Cost a year = two-way turnover × 10bp. The 2023–2026 total of 0.39% is the same cost, on the same trades, that appears as the −0.4% trading-cost line in Sources of the Alpha. Changing long names falls from 141% to 98% a year after 2023 because the long book has held more names since then (11 on average, against as few as one in 2019), so each quarterly rebalance replaces a smaller share of it.

Turnover measures how much is traded in a year relative to the portfolio's capital. Two-way counts every purchase and every sale: each day, the absolute change in every position's weight is added up, and the daily sums are totalled and annualised. One-way — the convention in fund prospectuses, including the ETF figures above — counts roughly one side, the lesser of purchases or sales, so it is about half the two-way figure. On the one-way convention the strategy trades like an active fundamental long/short fund or a systematic factor fund (typically 100–600% a year), not like an index ETF.

Even at twice our assumed trading cost, or with a 2% management fee, the strategy keeps a Sharpe well above every benchmark's.

Even after a full "2 and 20" fee, the strategy beats GRID since 2023 on all three measures in the table:

  • Return: 28.7% a year against 23.0%.
  • Sharpe: 1.58 against 0.93.
  • Max drawdown: −9.9% against −20.8%.

Strategy Suitability, Risks and Mitigants#

risk mitigant
Thin long book. The long book holds 15 names today and 11 on average since 2023, and fell as low as one name at a 2019 rebalance. The October 2026 keyword clean-up removed about two names on average. A few names drive a large share of the return. The hold buffer (a held name stays while in the top 65%) keeps the book from shrinking at each rebalance. Planned: test a wider universe to raise the name count.
The tight-grid environment may end. The strategy is built for a grid short of capacity. Once new capacity catches up with demand, it will outlive its usefulness. The strategy has three partial/gradual mechanisms to adjust for this eventuality: i) when book is likely near peak, partially switch to T-bills, ii) target 20% vol so that if there is a sharp change to an oversupplied grid regime the strategy starts to scale back, iii) long book requires growing revenue. If that stops then we will shift endogenously to tbills. There is also the option to have a step-aside so that when real revenue growth drops below zero or real yield is below zero, we fully switch into t-bills
